1:
Henry begins by asking why the story is in the Bible at all, and Wesley repeats him almost word for word: we should not have had this account of Pharaoh's butler and baker recorded in scripture if it had not been serviceable to Joseph's preferment, for the world stands for the sake of the church and is governed for its good. From the fall of the two officers Henry draws his moral — high places are slippery places, and nothing is more uncertain than the favour of princes, whereas those who make God's favour their happiness will find him a better Master than Pharaoh, and not so extreme to mark what they do amiss. What the men had actually done neither he nor anyone else can say. Many conjectures there are, he reports: some make the offence no less than an attempt to take away the king's life, others no more than the casual lighting of a fly into his cup and a little sand into his bread; whatever it was, Providence by this means brought them into the prison where Joseph was. Clarke inclines to the graver guess, that they had probably been accused of attempting the king's life, the one by poisoning his drink and the other his bread.

On the rank of the two prisoners the voices agree and add detail from different quarters. Calvin insists we are not to understand any common person of each rank, but those who presided over the rest, since they are soon afterwards called eunuchs or nobles: they were, in short, two of the chief men of the court. Clarke gives the words behind the offices, the butler being a cup-bearer, the same as the saky among the Arabians and Persians, and the baker rather a cook or confectioner; Ellicott adds, out of Wilkinson's work on the monuments, that the Egyptians had carried the art of making confectionery to very great perfection. Clarke also explains why such men went to that particular prison: according to Diodorus every officer of the ancient kings of Egypt was drawn from the most illustrious priestly families, no common person being permitted to serve in the king's presence, so that men of noble family, when accused, went naturally to the state prison. Gill notes that the captain of the guard in whose house they were confined is generally thought to be Potiphar himself, unless he had died and another was put into his room; and Calvin takes the same identification as evidence that Potiphar's anger had by now been mitigated, since without his consent the jailer could never have treated Joseph with such clemency.

That Joseph was set over them is the hinge of the chapter, and Henry reads it as the first thaw. The captain of the guard himself charged Joseph with them, which intimates that he began now to be reconciled to him and perhaps to be convinced of his innocence, though he durst not release him for fear of disobliging his wife — John Baptist must lose his head to please Herodias. Gill supposes Joseph was recommended to him by the keeper of the prison for his prudence and fidelity, and notes that some render the clause the other way, that he committed Joseph to be with them, as Jarchi interprets it, the three being put together not merely for company but that Joseph might wait upon them. How long they lay there is left vague. Clarke observes that the word is literally days, that many suppose a complete year, and that Calmet, reckoning back from Pharaoh's birthday, supposed they had offended on the preceding one. Keil marks only what the interval ended in: after some time, and on the same night, these two prisoners each had a dream of his own, each one answering to the interpretation which specially applied to him.
5:
Gill notes first that it was not one dream between them but a dream apiece. Henry ascribes it to a special providence which filled the heads of these prisoners with unusual dreams, carrying with them evidences of a divine origin, and adds that God has immediate access to the spirits of men and can make them serviceable to his own purposes quite beyond the intention of those concerned. Clarke marks the difference from ordinary dreaming, the disordered working of a mind disturbed by disease or repletion; these had an interpretation, that is, were prophetic. Calvin argues the same point from the men's own reaction. Many frivolous things are presented to us which pass away and are forgotten, but some have the force and significance of prophecy; and unless the mark of a celestial oracle had been engraven upon these, the butler and the baker would never have fallen into such consternation of mind. Men are sometimes agitated by vain dreams, he grants, but there the terror subsides; here God had fixed an arrow in their minds which would not suffer them to rest.

What the dreams did to them, Henry states in a sentence Wesley reproduces almost word for word: it was not the prison that made them sad, for they were pretty well used to that, and perhaps lived jovially enough there, but the dream. God, they both conclude, has more ways than one to sadden the spirits of those that are to be made sad, and sinners hardy enough under outward troubles he can still reach by wounding their spirits. Gill notes that Joseph and they were in the same prison but not the same ward, and that he came in each morning, like a careful and faithful servant, to see that the prisoners in his charge were safe and to learn what they wanted. Henry makes much of what he did when he got there. Joseph was their keeper, and in that office he was mild; it becomes us to take cognizance of the sorrows even of those under our check, and it is some relief to men in trouble to be noticed. He was their companion in tribulation too, and communion in sufferings works compassion. Calvin turns the lesson back on the reader: men are softened by their own afflictions so that they do not despise others in misery, and such humanity has to be learned by experience.

Their complaint that there was no interpreter is explained by the place they were in. Clarke says they either had access to none or got no satisfactory meaning from those they asked; Ellicott is more precise: in Egypt the interpreting of dreams was the business of trained men, the magicians and wise men of the next chapter, and to such the prisoners could have no access — though Joseph denies that art and training can avail at all, and claims the interpretation for God. Keil reads the answer as a double move: he reminded them first that interpretations are God's and his gift, and then bade them tell him their dreams, from a consciousness, no doubt, that he was himself endowed with that gift. Calvin dates the gift precisely. By a new inspiration of the Spirit the power of prophecy, which he had not before possessed, was imparted to Joseph in the prison — when he had dreamed himself he remained in suspense about the revelation, whereas now he is a certain interpreter to others. Yet he claims nothing peculiar to God, offering his service only so far as his calling supplies the means; and Calvin contrasts Daniel, who by a larger measure of the Spirit could both recover a forgotten dream and expound it, with Joseph, to whom the half only of these gifts was given, who does not divine what they dreamed but confesses that it is hidden from him.
9:
Gill notes that the butler was forward to speak first, whereas the baker held back until he saw what a good interpretation the first dream received. What the dream shows about Egyptian drinking then divides the commentators. Clarke takes it as evidence that wine anciently was the mere expressed juice of the grape without fermentation, the cup-bearer taking the bunch, pressing the juice into the cup and instantly delivering it to his master. Keil warns against forcing the detail so far, since it must not be made to prove that the kings of Egypt drank only fresh juice: the cultivation of the vine and the drinking of wine among the Egyptians are established beyond question by ancient testimony and the earliest monuments, whatever Herodotus said. Ellicott takes the middle ground and reaches it from the other side. Plutarch's claim that before Psammetichus the Egyptians neither drank wine nor poured it out to the gods has been abundantly disproved, and probably arose from taking the custom of one district for the universal rule; nevertheless the king's drink here does not look like fermented wine but like a sort of sherbet of fresh grape-juice and water.

Ellicott finds a second Egyptian fingerprint in the dream's last words. The Hebrew says not into Pharaoh's hand but upon Pharaoh's palm, the hollow made by bending the fingers inwards; and where the Hebrews always spoke of placing a cup in a man's hand, as Joseph himself does a verse later, the Egyptian cup-bearer uses the idiom of his own country — Egyptian cups having no stems, but being flat bowls held in the very way he describes. Of the interpretation itself Calvin insists that Joseph does not offer what he thought probable, like some ambiguous conjecturer, but asserts the meaning by the revelation of the Spirit — for why say that the three branches are three days rather than anything else, unless the Spirit had suggested it? and by commending himself to the butler at once, as if the man were already restored, he shows how indubitable he held his own reading to be. Clarke seizes on the little word are, which here means signify: so this is my body means this bread represents my body, a form of speech frequent in scripture because the Hebrew has no proper word for signifies or represents.

That Joseph asked the butler to remember him has been held against him, and the entry's voices defend him on different grounds. Gill reports the charge in the Targum's words, that Joseph lost his superior confidence and retained the confidence of men, and answers that means are always to be used in subordination to the divine will. Calvin meets the objection that he sought a reward for prophecy: he did not set the gift of God to sale, but saw that a method of deliverance was now set before him by God which it was not lawful to refuse, since God, who from his childhood had twice promised him dominion, had not left him amid so many straits without consolation. Wesley, in words Henry had used before him, admires the modesty of the account: he does not reflect upon the brothers who sold him, saying only that he was stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, nor upon the mistress who persecuted him or the master who judged him, but mildly avers his own innocence — and when we are called to vindicate ourselves we should carefully avoid speaking ill of others. Ellicott reads the reticence as tactics as well as nobility. Joseph's purpose was to rouse the Egyptian's sympathy by letting him know he was free born and reduced to slavery by fraud; to have said that his sale was owing to family feuds would have done harm rather than good, and noble-minded men do not willingly reveal what is to the discredit of their relatives.
16:
Gill is careful about what the baker saw. The interpretation was good, he says, meaning not that it was right and just, though it was, but that it was agreeable and pleasing and portended well in the event; and it was that which drew the second dream out of a man who might otherwise have kept it to himself. Calvin says the same thing more sharply and turns it into a warning. The baker does not care about Joseph's skill and fidelity as an interpreter; it is because Joseph had brought good and useful tidings to his companion that he too desires an interpretation, hoping it will prove according to his mind. So, Calvin adds, many desire the word of God with ardour and alacrity, not because they simply wish to be governed by the Lord and to know what is right, but because they dream of mere enjoyment — and when the doctrine does not correspond with their wishes, they depart sorrowful and wounded.

Of the dream itself Gill notes that the bakemeats were all sorts of pastry, tarts and pies and the like, and reports from Josephus that two of the baskets were full of bread while the third held the various kinds of food usually prepared for kings. Keil observes that the carrying of the baskets upon the head is thoroughly Egyptian, and cites Herodotus for it. Gill adds that Joseph answered immediately, without any further thought or meditation, being divinely instructed. That is the point Calvin presses hardest. Though the explanation was about to prove unpleasant and severe, Joseph declared without ambiguity what had been revealed to him, and so executed with fidelity the office divinely committed to him; and this freedom, Calvin says, must be maintained by prophets and teachers, that they may not hesitate to inflict a wound by their teaching upon those whom God has sentenced to death. All love to be flattered, and the majority of teachers, wishing to yield to the corrupt wishes of the world, adulterate the word of God; no one is a sincere minister of it but he who, despising reproach, frames his teaching by God's command. Joseph would gladly have augured well of both men, but since it is not in his power to give a prosperous fortune to anyone, nothing remained but frankly to pronounce what he had received from the Lord.

The sentence turns on a phrase the chapter has already used once in the opposite sense. Ellicott puts the difference plainly: a few verses earlier the lifting up of the butler's head meant his elevation to his former rank, whereas here the significant addition from off thee implies that he would be beheaded and his body publicly exposed to ignominy. Calvin makes the same observation from the Hebrew, that the phrase by itself is ambiguous and may be taken in a good sense or a bad, so that the added words carry the whole weight — there seems to be an allusion of this kind, as if Joseph had said, Pharaoh will lift up thy head, that he may take it off. Gill gives the Targum's blunt paraphrase, that Pharaoh should remove his head from his body with a sword, and Clarke supplies the practice behind it: beheading, hanging and gibbeting were all modes of punishment among the ancient Egyptians, the criminal being beheaded first and then hung either on hooks or by the hands. Calvin ends on what the double fulfilment established. When Moses relates that what Joseph foretold happened to both men, he proves by that sign that Joseph was a true prophet of God; for though the prophets sometimes threatened punishments which God then abstained from inflicting, that was because a condition was annexed to such prophecies, whereas when the Lord speaks positively by his servants, whatever he predicts must be confirmed by the result.
20:
Gill pauses over what kind of birthday is meant, since the word could cover either the king's natural birth or the anniversary of his accession; he judges the natural birthday likelier, that being the Egyptian custom as it was the Persian. Clarke thinks the keeping of birthdays with a feast very ancient, and guesses it arose from a correct notion of the immortality of the soul, the commencement of life appearing of great consequence to one who believed he was to live for ever. Henry allows the custom, provided it is not abused as Jeroboam's and Herod's were, and turns it to use: we may all profitably take notice of our birthdays, with thankfulness for the mercies of our birth, sorrow for the sinfulness of it, and an expectation of the day of our death as better than the day of our birth. Calvin will not condemn the practice either, if only men would keep the right end in view and give thanks to God by whom they were created; but the world distorts what the fathers honestly instituted, so that most keep up the memory of God as the Author of their life as if their set purpose were to forget him.

The phrase that had carried opposite senses for the two men is now used of both at once, and the voices differ over what it means here. Wesley takes it as arraigned and tried them, and Clarke agrees, comparing the trial of Naboth, who was set on high among the people before the witnesses were produced; the issue was that the baker alone was found guilty while the butler was acquitted and restored. Ellicott thinks the phrase is more probably used to point out the exact fulfilment of Joseph's interpretation of the two dreams. Keil and Gill simply record the double outcome, the one given the cup back into his hand, the other hanged, as Joseph had said. Henry draws the moral of the speed of it — both were advanced, the one to his office and the other to the gallows, and both at the three days' end, so sudden are the revolutions of the wheel of nature.

On the forgetting itself all agree and then divide sharply over what to make of it. Gill notes that the butler said nothing that day nor for two years after, and calls it great ingratitude and the frequent character of courtiers, who in high places neglect both the petitions made to them and their own promises. Calvin adds a shrewder reason than mere forgetfulness, that the man did not dare mention Joseph lest he bring reproach on himself or trouble the king, since it is common with courtiers perfidiously to betray the innocent rather than offend those they are afraid of; and he finds the delay purposeful, teaching us that nothing is more improper than to prescribe the time in which God shall help us — had liberty come by the butler's entreaty, the benefit would have been credited to man and not to God. Henry then reports the old parallel with approval — Joseph's two fellow-prisoners answering to the two thieves crucified with Christ, one saved and one condemned, and the butler forgetting the man who said remember me, where the thief who said remember me was not forgotten. Clarke will have none of it. Many commentators, he says, have seen in every circumstance of Joseph's history a parallel to our blessed Lord, and he believes God never designed such parallels; he is astonished to find grave and judicious men forcing the features of truth into so distorted a shape, warns against attributing to God designs he never had, and holds the mischief of this system to be really incalculable, since it gives the irreligious a pretext to scoff at all spirituality.
